title: Working with Big Data
text:
What you need to know






ImportantFor the assessment



You won’t work with genuinely big data, or need DuckDB. You should be able to explain why large data cause problems, and how to change an approach as the data grow: chunking with map-reduce, or doing the work in a database (week 9).



The DuckDB demos today run on a 29GB file of US flight prices from Kaggle (notes/data/load_itineraries.sh downloads it). Each query takes about 20 seconds on a laptop — fill the time by asking the room to predict the result, or by talking about what DuckDB is doing (streaming through the file on disk, using every core).

title: Working with Big Data
text:
The three Vs


Volume: too much to store or load — terabytes, petabytes




Velocity: arrives faster than it can be processed — e.g. a live stream of every post on a social media site




Variety: many types and sources — tables, text, images, sensor data



“Big” is relative: it depends on your hardware and tools. What’s big for a laptop is routine for a cluster.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Why is it a problem?






ImportantTask



Our flight prices file is 29 GB. A typical laptop has 16 GB of memory. What happens if we run read_csv("data/itineraries.csv")?



read_csv loads the whole file into memory as a tibble — and it doesn’t fit. R fails, or the computer slows to a crawl as it swaps memory to disk.
But we don’t need it all in memory to compute, say, a mean: we could read each value once, keep a running total and a count, and throw the value away.

The workflow runs as fast as its bottleneck. Big data work is trading them off: reading in chunks uses less memory, but takes longer.


Storage speeds: a solid-state drive is far slower than memory, a spinning hard drive slower still. Compute: many cores, and GPUs, help when work can be split into independent pieces — at the cost of complexity.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Find the bottleneck






ImportantTask



What limits each of these? How would you cope?

Summarising a 1 TB CSV file on a laptop
Analysing a live stream of every post on a social media site





Storage: it can’t be loaded, so it must be read from disk in pieces (or loaded into a database). At ~500 MB/s, one pass through 1 TB takes over half an hour — so compute everything you need in as few passes as possible.
Compute (or the network): data may arrive faster than one machine can process it. Process each record as it arrives keeping running summaries, discard what you don’t need early, and share the work across many machines.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Is my data actually big?
Before reaching for special tools:

library(tidyverse)
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
format(object.size(penguins), units = "KB")

[1] "32.3 Kb"




fares <- read_csv(
  "data/itineraries.csv",
  col_select = c(startingAirport, baseFare),   # only the columns you need
  n_max = 100000                               # develop on a subset
)
format(object.size(fares), units = "MB")

[1] "1.5 Mb"




Check the file size on disk first: it’s a rough guide to the memory needed. n_max reads the first rows, which may not be representative of the rest — fine for writing and testing code, not for final results.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Better storage
A CSV must be read in full, even to get one column.


Relational databases (week 9): data on disk, indexes, powerful servers
Columnar formats — Parquet, Feather: each column stored together, so you read only the columns you need
HDF5: large arrays and scientific data, with fast access to subsets

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Beyond one computer

Hadoop: distributed storage (HDFS) and processing (MapReduce) across a cluster
Apache Spark: fast cluster computing, with APIs for R, Python, Scala, Java


R is often a layer on top of these, rather than the engine:

dbplyr — dplyr code run in a database (week 9)
sparklyr — dplyr code run on a Spark cluster
duckdb / duckplyr — a fast analytical database, in-process
readr::read_csv_chunked() — simple map-reduce in plain R

A database without a server
DuckDB runs inside your R session, and can query a CSV file on disk without loading it.

library(duckplyr)
flights <- read_csv_duckdb("data/itineraries.csv")


flights |> summarise(n = n())

# A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable
         n
     <int>
1 82138753



DEMO (optional): run these live — the count takes ~20 s on 82 million rows. Open Activity Monitor while it runs: memory barely moves, all CPU cores are busy. That’s the point.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Mean fare by airport






ImportantTask



Compute the mean baseFare for each startingAirport, the usual way.




flights |>
  group_by(startingAirport) |>
  summarise(mean_base_fare = mean(baseFare, na.rm = TRUE))

Error in `group_by()`:
! This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB, and the input is a
  stingy duckplyr frame.
* Try `summarise(.by = ...)` or `mutate(.by = ...)` instead of `group_by()` and
  `ungroup()`.
i Use `compute(prudence = "lavish")` to materialize to temporary storage and
  continue with duckplyr.
i See `vignette("prudence")` for other options.




Read the error out: duckplyr can’t run group_by() inside DuckDB, and rather than silently pulling 29 GB into R, it stops. The message tells you the fix. General lesson: these tools support most of dplyr; when something fails, the error message usually says how to rewrite it.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Same thing, with dbplyr

library(DBI)
library(dbplyr)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
flights_db <- duckdb::tbl_file(con, "data/itineraries.csv")

flights_db |>
  group_by(startingAirport) |>
  summarise(mean_base_fare = mean(baseFare, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  show_query()

<SQL>
SELECT startingAirport, AVG(baseFare) AS mean_base_fare
FROM (FROM 'data/itineraries.csv') q01
GROUP BY startingAirport



Exactly week 9 — a lazy table, translated to SQL — except the FROM names a CSV file. collect() would give the same 16 rows.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Split, summarise, combine





flowchart LR
  file[("itineraries.csv")] --> c1["chunk 1"] & c2["chunk 2"] & c3["..."]
  c1 --> s1["summary"]
  c2 --> s2["summary"]
  c3 --> s3["..."]
  s1 & s2 & s3 --> result["combine"]








map: process each chunk independently, keeping only a small summary
reduce: combine the summaries into the answer



Only one chunk in memory at a time — and in Hadoop, chunks are processed on many machines at once.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
What should each chunk return?






ImportantTask



To find the mean body mass of the penguins, we split the data into chunks of 100 rows. Why not just average the four chunk means?




mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
chunks <- split(mass, ceiling(seq_along(mass) / 100))
lengths(chunks)

  1   2   3   4 
100 100 100  44 

mean(map_dbl(chunks, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))   # mean of chunk means

[1] 4139.497

mean(mass, na.rm = TRUE)                            # the true mean

[1] 4201.754


The chunks have different sizes, so their means can’t simply be averaged. Return a sum and a count from each chunk: those can be added up.


General principle: the map step must return enough to combine the partial results exactly. Sums and counts add; means, medians don’t.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
Chunks in R

summarise_chunk <- function(chunk, pos) {          # map: one chunk
  chunk |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(sum_mass = sum(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
              n = sum(!is.na(body_mass_g)), .groups = "drop")
}

results <- read_csv_chunked(
  "data/penguins.csv",
  callback = DataFrameCallback$new(summarise_chunk),
  chunk_size = 100,
  col_types = cols_only(species = col_character(),
                        body_mass_g = col_double())
)

results |>                                          # reduce: combine
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = sum(sum_mass) / sum(n))

# A tibble: 3 x 2
  species   mean_mass
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 Adelie        3701.
2 Chinstrap     3733.
3 Gentoo        5076.



results has one row per species per chunk; the reduce adds up the sums and counts. This is reduce() with an .init accumulator from week 8, in disguise. Exactly the same code, with chunk_size = 50000, computes the mean fare per airport from the 29 GB file — the notes show the output; it takes a long time, so don’t run it live.

title: Working with Big Data
text:
A chunking trap






ImportantTask



A file’s code column holds numbers for 15 rows, then codes like A1. We read it in chunks of 10 rows. What happens to the last five codes?



csv_text <- I(paste(
  c("id,code", paste0(1:20, ",", c(1:15, paste0("A", 1:5)))),
  collapse = "\n"
))
read_chunk <- DataFrameCallback$new(function(chunk, pos) chunk)



read_csv_chunked(csv_text, read_chunk, chunk_size = 10,
                 show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  tail(6)

# A tibble: 6 x 2
     id  code
  <dbl> <dbl>
1    15    15
2    16    NA
3    17    NA
4    18    NA
5    19    NA
6    20    NA


Column types are guessed from the first chunk only: code looks numeric, so later text becomes NA — silently. Always give col_types.

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Packages and data

library(tidyverse)   # includes purrr
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")


purrr is part of the tidyverse: it’s the package for functional programming and iteration.

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Scripts don’t stay scripts
A script: written quickly, to answer one question, run once by its author.

Research software: code that others — or you, in six months — rely on. It’s re-run on new data, extended, shared, and its results get published.


“Can you re-run it on next year’s data?” → “…with one variable changed?” → “…and update the plots for the paper?”


Research software engineering (RSE): applying software engineering principles so that code is robust, reusable and maintainable.


Ask the room: who has had to re-run an analysis they wrote weeks ago? If the code is one long file with hard-coded paths and copy-pasted blocks, every request means editing several places and hoping nothing breaks — and nobody is sure the published numbers came from the code as it stands now. Week 3 (Quarto, git) was the first half of RSE; today is about structure.

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Four principles


Separation of concerns — each part has one job: load, clean, model, plot, report




Modularity — build the parts as independent, reusable functions




Don’t repeat yourself (DRY) — every piece of knowledge written in exactly one place




Fail fast — check for problems early and stop with a clear error

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Separation of concerns


Everything mixed together
read_csv("data.csv") |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  mutate(y = log(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()

Clear separation
raw_data <- read_csv("data.csv")
clean_data <- clean_dataset(raw_data)
model <- fit_model(clean_data)
plot_results(model)



Longer to write — each function must be defined somewhere — but it reads as a summary of the analysis, each step can be checked on its own, and a change to cleaning means editing one function.

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Copy, paste, edit






ImportantTask



We want the same plot for Adelie penguins on two islands. What’s wrong here?


penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Biscoe") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Adelie penguins on Biscoe")
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelia", island == "Dream") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Adelie penguins on Dream")











A typo, "Adelia", crept in while editing the copy. R gives no error: filtering for a species that doesn’t exist is valid, and returns no rows — so the second plot is silently empty.


Let them look for 30 seconds before revealing. The general lesson: two copies of the same logic must be kept in step, and nothing warns us when they drift apart.

text:
Organising a project
my-project/

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Scripts don’t stay scripts
A script: written quickly, to answer one question, run once by its author.

Research software: code that others — or you, in six months — rely on. It’s re-run on new data, extended, shared, and its results get published.


“Can you re-run it on next year’s data?” → “…with one variable changed?” → “…and update the plots for the paper?”


Research software engineering (RSE): applying software engineering principles so that code is robust, reusable and maintainable.


Ask the room: who has had to re-run an analysis they wrote weeks ago? If the code is one long file with hard-coded paths and copy-pasted blocks, every request means editing several places and hoping nothing breaks — and nobody is sure the published numbers came from the code as it stands now. Week 3 (Quarto, git) was the first half of RSE; today is about structure.

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming
text:
Four principles


Separation of concerns — each part has one job: load, clean, model, plot, report




Modularity — build the parts as independent, reusable functions




Don’t repeat yourself (DRY) — every piece of knowledge written in exactly one place




Fail fast — check for problems early and stop with a clear error

title: Research Software Engineering and Functional Programming

Everything mixed together

  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  mutate(y = log(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()

Clear separation

clean_data <- clean_dataset(raw_data)
model <- fit_model(clean_data)
plot_results(model)


Longer to write — each function must be defined somewhere — but it reads as a summary of the analysis, each step can be checked on its own, and a change to cleaning means editing one function.

Task


We want the same plot for Adelie penguins on two islands. What’s wrong here?

  filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Biscoe") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Adelie penguins on Biscoe")

  filter(species == "Adelia", island == "Dream") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Adelie penguins on Dream")











A typo, "Adelia", crept in while editing the copy. R gives no error: filtering for a species that doesn’t exist is valid, and returns no rows — so the second plot is silently empty.


Let them look for 30 seconds before revealing. The general lesson: two copies of the same logic must be kept in step, and nothing warns us when they drift apart.

title: Data Ethics and Biases
text:
Amazon’s recruiting tool


Amazon built a tool to score job applicants’ CVs automatically




Training data: every CV submitted to the company over the previous ten years, and who was hired




By 2015 they found it was not gender neutral: given equally skilled applicants, it preferred men








ImportantTask



Why? The tool was never told the applicants’ gender.



It didn’t learn what makes a good candidate — it learned what Amazon’s past hires looked like, and past hiring in tech had favoured men (and most applicants were men).


Source: the Reuters report, linked from the notes. Let them discuss before revealing — someone usually gets there.

title: Data Ethics and Biases
text:
Removing gender isn’t enough
Amazon edited the tool to ignore the terms found to penalise women. It still couldn’t be trusted:


“captain of the women’s chess club”
all-women colleges
men and women describing their experience in different words



These are proxies: variables that stand in for an attribute that was removed. A postcode can be a proxy for ethnicity or income.


Amazon scrapped the tool.

title: Data Ethics and Biases
text:
It’s not just Amazon

COMPAS, used in some US courts to predict reoffending: a 2016 ProPublica investigation found Black defendants who did not reoffend were labelled high risk nearly twice as often as white defendants
Credit scoring: lower scores for freelancers and gig workers, whose income is documented differently — regardless of whether they are financially stable


We can’t prevent every bias. Our job: recognise it, mitigate it, and alert the people who rely on our work.

title: Data Ethics and Biases
text:
Six kinds of bias

Sampling: the sample doesn’t represent the population
Selection: whether a record appears depends on the outcome being studied

Amazon’s recruiting tool


Amazon built a tool to score job applicants’ CVs automatically




Training data: every CV submitted to the company over the previous ten years, and who was hired




By 2015 they found it was not gender neutral: given equally skilled applicants, it preferred men








Task


Why? The tool was never told the applicants’ gender.




It didn’t learn what makes a good candidate — it learned what Amazon’s past hires looked like, and past hiring in tech had favoured men (and most applicants were men).


Source: the Reuters report, linked from the notes. Let them discuss before revealing — someone usually gets there.

Amazon edited the tool to ignore the terms found to penalise women. It still couldn’t be trusted:


“captain of the women’s chess club”
all-women colleges
men and women describing their experience in different words



These are proxies: variables that stand in for an attribute that was removed. A postcode can be a proxy for ethnicity or income.


Amazon scrapped the tool.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Why not one big table?


Size: a flat table repeats every student’s name for every course




Integrity: a name change is made in one place




Flexibility: new tables (e.g. references) can link to students without touching grades




Clarity: the structure mirrors the real world — “each student takes many courses”



Keep this short — the point is that real data arrives split up on purpose, so joining is a routine step, not a workaround. The SQL week will return to this idea.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Two common surprises






Duplicated column names


If both tables have a non-key column with the same name (say notes), you get notes.x and notes.y. Control this with the suffix argument.









Many-to-many joins


If both tables have several rows per key, you get every combination — the row count can explode. dplyr warns you; it is usually a mistake.




Rule of thumb: check nrow() before and after every join.

Times and time zones






Task


A server logs an event at 2025-08-11 11:33:01 UTC. What did the clocks in Tokyo say at that moment?





t1 <- ymd_hms("2025-08-11 11:33:01")
tz(t1)

[1] "UTC"

with_tz(t1, "Asia/Tokyo")    # convert: read the same moment off a Tokyo clock

Same event, so only the displayed time changes: 11:33 UTC is 20:33 in Tokyo.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:

Task


A sensor in Tokyo wrote 2025-08-11 11:33:01 in Tokyo local time, but R read it as UTC. Correct the time zone.

t2

[1] "2025-08-11 11:33:01 JST"

t2 - t1                            # a genuinely different moment

Time difference of -9 hours

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Time Zone Summary




Clock shows
Is it the same event?




with_tz()
changes (11:33 → 20:33)
yes — just viewed from Tokyo


force_tz()
stays 11:33
no — now 9 hours earlier



Use with_tz() to view a correct time somewhere else. Use force_tz() only to fix a time that was recorded with the wrong zone.

Two common surprises






WarningDuplicated column names



If both tables have a non-key column with the same name (say notes), you get notes.x and notes.y. Control this with the suffix argument.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Objectives
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:


explain what Shiny is, and what problem it solves




describe how a Shiny app is structured — a ui and a server — and run one




describe reactive programming at a high level: sources, conductors and endpoints




recognise the common input, output and layout components, and Shiny’s main uses and limitations



All of today’s apps are in slides/apps/week07/ (also linked from the handout). Open RStudio with that folder before the lecture, so each demo is one click on “Run App”. Run each app from its own file so that the working directory is the app’s folder (app4_explorer.R reads data/penguins.csv).

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Sharing an analysis
So far, our results reach other people as static reports: they see the plots and tables we chose.

Shiny is an R package for building interactive web apps entirely in R:

users change the inputs (e.g. choose a subset, move a slider) and the results update in their browser
you write only R; Shiny generates the website (HTML, CSS and JavaScript)



The audience: people who don’t program in R.


Open the gallery examples now, briefly (1–2 min total):

Movie Explorer — filters and selectors over a films dataset.
Radiant — an entire statistics package built as a Shiny app.

The point: everything they have done so far in the course could sit behind an app like this.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Setting up
install.packages("shiny")   # once, in the console
library(shiny)              # at the top of every app script


shiny is not part of the tidyverse
apps are written in .R scripts, not .qmd files — a rendered Quarto document is a static web page, with no R running behind it
convention: one script, app.R, ending in shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Introduction to Shiny
Introduction to Shiny
text:
Hello Shiny: running


DEMO: open app1_hello.R and click “Run App”. Move the slider and watch the text update. Resize the window to show the layout adapting.
Stop the app (red stop icon) before moving on — the console is busy while an app runs.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
The naming contract






Task


How does the server know which slider to read, and where to put the text?




By name:







In the UI
In the server




sliderInput("num", ...)
read it as input$num


textOutput("result")
fill it with output$result <- renderText(...)



Every input’s first argument is its name; every output’s name must match an output$... assignment.


This is the backbone of every app. A mismatched output name gives no error — the output just stays blank. That’s the most common silent bug; we’ll come back to it.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Add an output






Task


Extend the app so that it also shows the square of the chosen number.




# in the UI, inside mainPanel(), after a comma:
textOutput("result"),
textOutput("squared")

# in the server:
output$squared <- renderText({
  paste("Its square is:", input$num^2)
})


Two changes, joined by a name: a slot in the UI, and a render* function in the server.


Do this live in app1_hello.R. Deliberately forget the comma after textOutput("result") first and run it: the error is unexpected symbol, pointing at the component after the gap. The UI is one big nested function call, so every component needs a comma. (A trailing comma after the last one is harmless.)

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Running an app
Three ways to start it:

define ui and server, then run shinyApp(ui, server)
save as app.R and call runApp() (or runApp("path/to/app"))
click Run App in RStudio


Listening on http://127.0.0.1:3689
Shiny starts a web server on your computer. The browser and the R process stay connected: each change to an input is sent to R, which sends back updated outputs.


While the app runs your console is busy — stop it (stop icon, or Esc) to get your prompt back.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Does the server re-run?






Task


When the user moves the slider, which code runs again?




Not the whole server function — only the renderText({...}) block, because it reads input$num, which has changed.


Shiny keeps a reactive graph: a record of which code reads which values. When a value changes, it re-runs only what depends on it.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Three roles in the graph








Role
Created with
Read with




Source
*Input("x", ...) in the UI
input$x


Source
x <- reactiveVal(initial)
x(); set with x(new_value)


Conductor
x <- reactive({...})
x()


Endpoint (output)
output$x <- render*({...})
displayed by *Output("x")


Endpoint (observer)
observe({...}), observeEvent(e, {...})
not read: run for side effects




Sources hold values that change; conductors compute from them; endpoints have an effect — update the page, or do something.


The Hello app is the smallest possible graph: one source (input$num) straight into one endpoint (output$result). reactiveValues() is a third kind of source, a list-like version of reactiveVal; it’s in the notes.

title: Introduction to Shiny
Introduction to Shiny
text:
A conductor: running


DEMO: run app2_samples.R. Change mu1: the cloud moves and the means update. Then type in the name box: only the greeting changes, the points stay exactly where they are. Leave the question of why to the next slide.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Draw the graph






Task


Draw the reactive graph of this app. What re-runs when you change \(\mu_1\)? When you type a new name?















Changing \(\mu_1\) re-runs samples(), the plot and the means. Typing a name re-runs only the greeting.


Point out that samples() is computed once per change even though two endpoints call it: the first caller recomputes it, the second gets the cached result.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Why not skip the conductor?






Task


Why not just call rnorm() inside each render* block?




Each output would draw its own sample: the means printed under the plot would describe different points from the ones plotted.
A reactive() computes the sample once and caches it, so every output sees the same data — and it is only recomputed when input$mu1 or input$mu2 changes.


If asked: putting set.seed() at the top of the reactive makes each redraw use the same random numbers, so changing mu1 just slides the cloud (links back to week 3’s reproducibility).

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Spot the bugs






Task


Each line below is inside server. Each fails. Why?



mean_x1 <- mean(samples()$x1)                      # (a)
output$means <- renderText(mean(samples$x1))       # (b)
input$mu1 <- 0                                     # (c)


reactive values can only be read inside reactive code (reactive, render*, observe*): “Operation not allowed without an active reactive context”.
missing parentheses: samples is a function, so samples$x1 gives “object of type ‘closure’ is not subsettable”. Use samples()$x1.
inputs are read-only — the user sets them. If the server needs a value it can change, use reactiveVal().

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Observers: making things happen
Rule of thumb:

compute a value for other code to use → reactive()
make something happen → an observer



observe({...}) re-runs when anything it reads changes
observeEvent(event, {...}) re-runs only when event changes



observe({
  message("mu1 is now ", input$mu1)   # prints to the R console
})
A cheap way to watch the graph at work — and a useful debugging trick.

Components








Layout
Inputs
Outputs (UI ↔︎ server)




fluidPage()
sliderInput()
textOutput() ↔︎ renderText()


titlePanel()
selectInput()
plotOutput() ↔︎ renderPlot()


sidebarLayout()
numericInput(), textInput()

uiOutput() ↔︎ renderUI()

Open the widget gallery briefly to show it’s runnable. Mention tabsets and sortable tables with the DT package. Newer Shiny docs use bslib layouts (page_sidebar(), card()): same idea, more modern look; we stick with fluidPage.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
A penguin explorer






Task


Plan an app for the penguins data: the user picks a species and a range of body mass, and sees a scatter plot of body mass against flipper length, with an optional trend line, plus a table giving the number of penguins and their mean mass. Nothing should be shown until a species is chosen.
Which inputs? Which outputs? What should be a reactive()?





inputs: selectInput (species, with an empty first choice), sliderInput with a length-two value (a range), checkboxInput (trend line)
outputs: plotOutput + tableOutput
one reactive() for the filtered data, read by both outputs
req(input$species) in each render*: produce nothing until a species is chosen

title: Introduction to Shiny
Introduction to Shiny
text:
The explorer: running


DEMO: run app4_explorer.R. Show the blank page before a species is picked (that’s req), then pick Gentoo, drag the range slider, untick the trend.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
When it goes wrong


Missing comma in the UI → unexpected symbol
Mismatched output name → no error, the output is just blank: compare the names character by character
Error inside a render* → the app keeps running, the output shows the error; the console shows Warning: Error in ...



To look inside a running app:

message() / print() in the server write to the console
browser() inside a reactive block pauses the app there: inspect input$species or selected(), then c to continue, Q to quit



If there’s time, demo browser() in app4_explorer.R: put it as the first line of selected(), re-run, choose a species, and inspect input$mass at the prompt.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:

The naming contract






ImportantTask



How does the server know which slider to read, and where to put the text?



By name:







In the UI
In the server




sliderInput("num", ...)
read it as input$num


textOutput("result")
fill it with output$result <- renderText(...)



Every input’s first argument is its name; every output’s name must match an output$... assignment.


This is the backbone of every app. A mismatched output name gives no error — the output just stays blank. That’s the most common silent bug; we’ll come back to it.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Add an output






ImportantTask



Extend the app so that it also shows the square of the chosen number.



# in the UI, inside mainPanel(), after a comma:
textOutput("result"),
textOutput("squared")

# in the server:
output$squared <- renderText({
  paste("Its square is:", input$num^2)
})


Two changes, joined by a name: a slot in the UI, and a render* function in the server.


Do this live in app1_hello.R. Deliberately forget the comma after textOutput("result") first and run it: the error is unexpected symbol, pointing at the component after the gap. The UI is one big nested function call, so every component needs a comma. (A trailing comma after the last one is harmless.)

text:
Running an app
Three ways to start it:

define ui and server, then run shinyApp(ui, server)
save as app.R and call runApp() (or runApp("path/to/app"))
click Run App in RStudio


Listening on http://127.0.0.1:3689
Shiny starts a web server on your computer. The browser and the R process stay connected: each change to an input is sent to R, which sends back updated outputs.


While the app runs your console is busy — stop it (stop icon, or Esc) to get your prompt back.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Does the server re-run?






ImportantTask



When the user moves the slider, which code runs again?



Not the whole server function — only the renderText({...}) block, because it reads input$num, which has changed.


Shiny keeps a reactive graph: a record of which code reads which values. When a value changes, it re-runs only what depends on it.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Three roles in the graph








Role
Created with
Read with




Source
*Input("x", ...) in the UI
input$x


Source
x <- reactiveVal(initial)
x(); set with x(new_value)


Conductor
x <- reactive({...})
x()


Endpoint (output)
output$x <- render*({...})
displayed by *Output("x")


Endpoint (observer)
observe({...}), observeEvent(e, {...})
not read: run for side effects




Sources hold values that change; conductors compute from them; endpoints have an effect — update the page, or do something.


The Hello app is the smallest possible graph: one source (input$num) straight into one endpoint (output$result). reactiveValues() is a third kind of source, a list-like version of reactiveVal; it’s in the notes.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Draw the graph






ImportantTask



Draw the reactive graph of this app. What re-runs when you change \(\mu_1\)? When you type a new name?








flowchart LR
  mu1["input$mu1"] --> samples["samples()"]
  mu2["input$mu2"] --> samples
  samples --> plot["output$plot"]
  samples --> means["output$means"]
  name["input$name"] --> greeting["output$greeting"]






Changing \(\mu_1\) re-runs samples(), the plot and the means. Typing a name re-runs only the greeting.


Point out that samples() is computed once per change even though two endpoints call it: the first caller recomputes it, the second gets the cached result.

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Why not skip the conductor?






ImportantTask



Why not just call rnorm() inside each render* block?



Each output would draw its own sample: the means printed under the plot would describe different points from the ones plotted.
A reactive() computes the sample once and caches it, so every output sees the same data — and it is only recomputed when input$mu1 or input$mu2 changes.


If asked: putting set.seed() at the top of the reactive makes each redraw use the same random numbers, so changing mu1 just slides the cloud (links back to week 3’s reproducibility).

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Spot the bugs






ImportantTask



Each line below is inside server. Each fails. Why?


mean_x1 <- mean(samples()$x1)                      # (a)
output$means <- renderText(mean(samples$x1))       # (b)
input$mu1 <- 0                                     # (c)


reactive values can only be read inside reactive code (reactive, render*, observe*): “Operation not allowed without an active reactive context”.
missing parentheses: samples is a function, so samples$x1 gives “object of type ‘closure’ is not subsettable”. Use samples()$x1.
inputs are read-only — the user sets them. If the server needs a value it can change, use reactiveVal().

title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Observers: making things happen
Rule of thumb:

compute a value for other code to use → reactive()
make something happen → an observer



observe({...}) re-runs when anything it reads changes
observeEvent(event, {...}) re-runs only when event changes



observe({
  message("mu1 is now ", input$mu1)   # prints to the R console
})
A cheap way to watch the graph at work — and a useful debugging trick.

text:
Objectives
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:


explain what a relational database adds to a folder of CSV files




read SQL queries — including joins, GROUP BY and subqueries — and say what they return




decide whether work should be done in the database or in R, and use dbplyr to query a database with dplyr code



Set expectations early: students will not be asked to write SQL. They must be able to read it, and to work with databases from R via dbplyr. Today’s SQL is all run against a small database built from the student tables of week 5.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
CSV files
Until now, all our data has come from CSV files:


a flat table of text
no types — R has to guess them
no validation of what goes in
no way to say how one file relates to another

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Remember week 5?






Task


student_grades.csv contains grades for students 21 and 22, who don’t appear in student_data.csv. Should that be possible? Could a CSV file stop it?




It shouldn’t be possible: a grade must belong to a student. But a CSV file is just text — nothing checks it. We only found the problem by joining.
A relational database can refuse to store it in the first place.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Relational databases
A database holds tables (like data frames), plus rules about them:


every column has a type, checked on the way in
a primary key uniquely identifies each row (e.g. a student’s id)
a foreign key must match a primary key in another table (each grade’s student_id must be a real student)



We talk to it in SQL (Structured Query Language). SQL is declarative: you say what you want, and the database works out how.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Why use one?


Integrity: types and keys keep data consistent
Scale: data lives on disk, not in memory; the server may be far more powerful than your laptop
Security: access controls and permissions
Concurrent access: many users reading and writing safely
Less duplication: related tables instead of one big one (week 5)



PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle… we use SQLite: a single file, no server. Each system has its own dialect of SQL.


Optional demo (2–3 min): open notes/data/customers.db in DB Browser for SQLite. Show the tables, their column types and the foreign keys under “Database Structure”. Point out it is not a plain-text file. Non-relational (“NoSQL”) databases such as MongoDB exist too, but are out of scope.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Creating tables

CREATE TABLE students (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    given_name TEXT,
    family_name TEXT,
    date_of_birth INTEGER
);


CREATE TABLE grades (
    student_id INTEGER,
    course TEXT,
    grade REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id)
);


Types are declared up front. AUTOINCREMENT generates new IDs; the FOREIGN KEY ties each grade to a student. Keywords are in CAPITALS by convention; comments start with --.


Behind the scenes, the 20 students and their grades from week 5 have been inserted — except the grades for the non-existent students 21 and 22. SQLite only checks foreign keys if you switch it on (PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON), which we have done; database servers check them by default.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Inserting a bad row






Task


What happens if we try to store a grade for student 21?




INSERT INTO grades(student_id, course, grade) VALUES (21, 'MATH6195', 70);




Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed


The database refuses it. The problem from week 5 can’t happen.

JOIN






Task


What does this return? Which students are missing from it?




SELECT students.given_name, students.family_name,
       grades.course, grades.grade

table.column says which table each column comes from.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Changing data

UPDATE grades
SET grade = 100
WHERE student_id = 15 AND course = 'MATH6195';


DELETE FROM grades
WHERE course = 'MATH2011';


Create (INSERT), Read (SELECT), Update, Delete: CRUD. Note the WHERE — without it, every row is updated or deleted.


DROP TABLE deletes a whole table and its data. These statements change the database permanently — there’s no undo.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
GROUP BY






Task


What does this return?




SELECT course, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(grade) AS mean_grade
FROM grades
GROUP BY course;





2 records


course

One row per course, with its number of grades and mean grade — group_by() then summarise(). AS names a calculated column. (MATH2011 is gone: we just deleted it.)


Every column in the SELECT must either be in the GROUP BY or be an aggregate like COUNT, SUM, AVG. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-missing values. Missing values in SQL are NULL; aggregates skip them, as if na.rm = TRUE.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Subqueries






Task


What does this return? Read the inner query first.




SELECT given_name, family_name
FROM students
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT student_id
    FROM grades
    GROUP BY student_id
    HAVING AVG(grade) > 75
);

The inner query finds the IDs of students whose average grade is over 75; the outer query looks up their names. HAVING filters groups; IN compares against a list.


NOT IN works too: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM grades) finds student 7 — the anti_join() of week 5. The notes describe a trap: if the subquery returns a NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all, silently.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
How to read a query
Written in a fixed order, starting with SELECT — but run in this order:



FROM, JOIN
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
SELECT
DISTINCT
ORDER BY
LIMIT



So start reading at FROM.
This explains the rules: WHERE runs before grouping, so it can’t use COUNT(*) — that’s what HAVING is for.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
SQL to dplyr






Task


Rewrite this query as a dplyr pipeline on a tibble grades.



SELECT student_id, COUNT(*) AS n_courses
FROM grades
WHERE grade >= 60
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY n_courses DESC
LIMIT 5;

grades |>
  filter(grade >= 60) |>               # WHERE
  group_by(student_id) |>              # GROUP BY
  summarise(n_courses = n()) |>        # SELECT ... COUNT(*) AS
  filter(n_courses > 1) |>             # HAVING
  arrange(desc(n_courses)) |>          # ORDER BY ... DESC
  head(5)                              # LIMIT
The dplyr steps appear in the order SQL runs them.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Where should the work happen?
In the database, importing only the result:

less data to transfer — a summary of millions of rows may be a few rows
data larger than memory
speed: databases are built for this
privacy: individual-level data never leaves the database


In R, after importing the tables:

R can do far more: models, plots, packages
simpler when the data are small



Usually both: the database filters, joins and summarises; R does the rest.

dbplyr

students <- tbl(con, "students")   # con: made with dbConnect()

dplyr in, SQL out






Task


Use dplyr to find each course’s number of grades and mean grade. Then look at the SQL that dbplyr writes.





query <- grades |>
  group_by(course) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_grade = mean(grade, na.rm = TRUE))

show_query(query)

collect()

class(query)

[1] "tbl_SQLiteConnection" "tbl_dbi"              "tbl_sql"             
[4] "tbl_lazy"             "tbl"

1 MATH2010    17       64.5
2 MATH6195    18       69.2



Nothing runs until collect() (or printing). collect() runs the SQL in the database and brings the result into R as a tibble.


sql_render(query) returns the SQL as a string, so it can be passed to dbGetQuery() to check it — in the notes.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Collect as late as possible






Task


Both give the same answer. Which is better, and why?



grades |> filter(grade > 80) |> collect()
grades |> collect() |> filter(grade > 80)

The first: the filter runs in the database, and only matching rows are sent to R. The second transfers the whole table, then throws most of it away. On millions of rows, that’s seconds versus not fitting in memory.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Limits of the translation

students |>
  mutate(padded = stringr::str_pad(given_name, 10)) |>
  collect()

Error in `stringr::str_pad()`:
! `str_pad()` is not available in this SQL variant.



Only functions dbplyr can translate to SQL work before collect(). Do what you can in the database, collect(), then use the rest of R.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Joining

prizes <- tibble(id = c(11, 6), prize = c("Gold", "Silver"))
students |> inner_join(prizes, by = "id")

Error in `auto_copy()`:
! `x` and `y` must share the same src.
i `x` is a <tbl_SQLiteConnection/tbl_dbi/tbl_sql/tbl_lazy/tbl> object.
i `y` is a <tbl_df/tbl/data.frame> object.
i Set `copy = TRUE` if `y` can be copied to the same source as `x` (may be
  slow).



A lazy table can only join to tables in the same database. Either copy = TRUE (copy the tibble into the database), or collect() first:

students |>
  inner_join(prizes, by = "id", copy = TRUE) |>
  select(given_name, family_name, prize) |>
  collect()

# A tibble: 2 x 3
  given_name family_name   prize 
  <chr>      <chr>         <chr> 
1 Tariq      Ibn Rashid    Gold  
2 Rajesh     Krishnamurthy Silver




Joining two lazy tables in the same database works just like dplyr: grades |> inner_join(students, by = c("student_id" = "id")). Finish with dbDisconnect(con) to close the connection.

Set expectations early: students will not be asked to write SQL. They must be able to read it, and to work with databases from R via dbplyr. Today’s SQL is all run against a small database built from the student tables of week 5.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
CSV files
Until now, all our data has come from CSV files:


a flat table of text
no types — R has to guess them
no validation of what goes in
no way to say how one file relates to another

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Remember week 5?






ImportantTask



student_grades.csv contains grades for students 21 and 22, who don’t appear in student_data.csv. Should that be possible? Could a CSV file stop it?



It shouldn’t be possible: a grade must belong to a student. But a CSV file is just text — nothing checks it. We only found the problem by joining.
A relational database can refuse to store it in the first place.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Relational databases
A database holds tables (like data frames), plus rules about them:


every column has a type, checked on the way in
a primary key uniquely identifies each row (e.g. a student’s id)
a foreign key must match a primary key in another table (each grade’s student_id must be a real student)



We talk to it in SQL (Structured Query Language). SQL is declarative: you say what you want, and the database works out how.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Why use one?


Integrity: types and keys keep data consistent
Scale: data lives on disk, not in memory; the server may be far more powerful than your laptop
Security: access controls and permissions
Concurrent access: many users reading and writing safely
Less duplication: related tables instead of one big one (week 5)



PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle… we use SQLite: a single file, no server. Each system has its own dialect of SQL.


Optional demo (2–3 min): open notes/data/customers.db in DB Browser for SQLite. Show the tables, their column types and the foreign keys under “Database Structure”. Point out it is not a plain-text file. Non-relational (“NoSQL”) databases such as MongoDB exist too, but are out of scope.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Creating tables

CREATE TABLE students (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    given_name TEXT,
    family_name TEXT,
    date_of_birth INTEGER
);


CREATE TABLE grades (
    student_id INTEGER,
    course TEXT,
    grade REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id)
);


Types are declared up front. AUTOINCREMENT generates new IDs; the FOREIGN KEY ties each grade to a student. Keywords are in CAPITALS by convention; comments start with --.


Behind the scenes, the 20 students and their grades from week 5 have been inserted — except the grades for the non-existent students 21 and 22. SQLite only checks foreign keys if you switch it on (PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON), which we have done; database servers check them by default.

Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed


The database refuses it. The problem from week 5 can’t happen.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Changing data

UPDATE grades
SET grade = 100
WHERE student_id = 15 AND course = 'MATH6195';


DELETE FROM grades
WHERE course = 'MATH2011';


Create (INSERT), Read (SELECT), Update, Delete: CRUD. Note the WHERE — without it, every row is updated or deleted.


DROP TABLE deletes a whole table and its data. These statements change the database permanently — there’s no undo.

GROUP BY






ImportantTask



What does this return?



SELECT course, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(grade) AS mean_grade
FROM grades
GROUP BY course;

One row per course, with its number of grades and mean grade — group_by() then summarise(). AS names a calculated column. (MATH2011 is gone: we just deleted it.)


Every column in the SELECT must either be in the GROUP BY or be an aggregate like COUNT, SUM, AVG. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-missing values. Missing values in SQL are NULL; aggregates skip them, as if na.rm = TRUE.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Subqueries






ImportantTask



What does this return? Read the inner query first.



SELECT given_name, family_name
FROM students
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT student_id
    FROM grades
    GROUP BY student_id
    HAVING AVG(grade) > 75
);





4 records

The inner query finds the IDs of students whose average grade is over 75; the outer query looks up their names. HAVING filters groups; IN compares against a list.


NOT IN works too: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM grades) finds student 7 — the anti_join() of week 5. The notes describe a trap: if the subquery returns a NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all, silently.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
How to read a query
Written in a fixed order, starting with SELECT — but run in this order:



FROM, JOIN
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
SELECT
DISTINCT
ORDER BY
LIMIT



So start reading at FROM.
This explains the rules: WHERE runs before grouping, so it can’t use COUNT(*) — that’s what HAVING is for.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
SQL to dplyr






ImportantTask



Rewrite this query as a dplyr pipeline on a tibble grades.


SELECT student_id, COUNT(*) AS n_courses
FROM grades
WHERE grade >= 60
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY n_courses DESC
LIMIT 5;

grades |>
  filter(grade >= 60) |>               # WHERE
  group_by(student_id) |>              # GROUP BY
  summarise(n_courses = n()) |>        # SELECT ... COUNT(*) AS
  filter(n_courses > 1) |>             # HAVING
  arrange(desc(n_courses)) |>          # ORDER BY ... DESC
  head(5)                              # LIMIT
The dplyr steps appear in the order SQL runs them.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Where should the work happen?
In the database, importing only the result:

less data to transfer — a summary of millions of rows may be a few rows
data larger than memory
speed: databases are built for this
privacy: individual-level data never leaves the database


In R, after importing the tables:

R can do far more: models, plots, packages
simpler when the data are small



Usually both: the database filters, joins and summarises; R does the rest.

  group_by(course) |>

Nothing runs until collect() (or printing). collect() runs the SQL in the database and brings the result into R as a tibble.


sql_render(query) returns the SQL as a string, so it can be passed to dbGetQuery() to check it — in the notes.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Collect as late as possible






ImportantTask



Both give the same answer. Which is better, and why?


grades |> filter(grade > 80) |> collect()
grades |> collect() |> filter(grade > 80)

The first: the filter runs in the database, and only matching rows are sent to R. The second transfers the whole table, then throws most of it away. On millions of rows, that’s seconds versus not fitting in memory.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Limits of the translation

students |>
  mutate(padded = stringr::str_pad(given_name, 10)) |>
  collect()

Error in `stringr::str_pad()`:
! `str_pad()` is not available in this SQL variant.



Only functions dbplyr can translate to SQL work before collect(). Do what you can in the database, collect(), then use the rest of R.

title: SQL for Data Science
text:
Joining

prizes <- tibble(id = c(11, 6), prize = c("Gold", "Silver"))
students |> inner_join(prizes, by = "id")

Error in `auto_copy()`:
! `x` and `y` must share the same src.
i `x` is a <tbl_SQLiteConnection/tbl_dbi/tbl_sql/tbl_lazy/tbl> object.
i `y` is a <tbl_df/tbl/data.frame> object.
i Set `copy = TRUE` if `y` can be copied to the same source as `x` (may be
  slow).



A lazy table can only join to tables in the same database. Either copy = TRUE (copy the tibble into the database), or collect() first:

students |>
  inner_join(prizes, by = "id", copy = TRUE) |>
  select(given_name, family_name, prize) |>
  collect()

# A tibble: 2 x 3
  given_name family_name   prize 
  <chr>      <chr>         <chr> 
1 Tariq      Ibn Rashid    Gold  
2 Rajesh     Krishnamurthy Silver




Joining two lazy tables in the same database works just like dplyr: grades |> inner_join(students, by = c("student_id" = "id")). Finish with dbDisconnect(con) to close the connection.
